hook: Epictetus sorted every worry into two piles. Can you?
title: Up to Me, or Not?

items.why: Timetables, weather, signals. Real, but not in your hands.
Your choice, fully. This is where the energy should go.

items.text: What your teacher, boss or family thinks of your idea
items.why: You can shape it, but their mind is theirs. Aim at the pitch, not the verdict.

items.text: How clearly you explain your idea
items.why: Preparation and clarity are yours. That's the part worth practising.
Opponents, luck and refs get a vote. The Stoics called outcomes 'not up to us'.

items.text: How hard you train this week
items.why: Training is your choice. How your body responds isn't: Epictetus put the body in 'not up to us'.

items.text: Your first emotional jolt when insulted
items.why: Seneca called these 'first movements': automatic, not chosen. The next minute is yours.

insight: Epictetus taught that suffering grows when we pour effort into the 'not up to me' pile. The trick: almost every outcome you can't control has an action next to it that you can.
model: Care about outcomes, but aim your effort at your own choices, judgments and actions.
try_today: Write your biggest worry. Under it, list two actions that are fully up to you. Do one before tonight.

source.work: Epictetus, Enchiridion (c. 125 CE); Seneca, On Anger II

try_team: Each person names one worry. Together sort it into 'up to us' and 'not up to us', then pick one 'up to us' action to do this week.

from_source.quote: Of things, some are in our power, and others not.

hook: Your flight is cancelled. 200 angry people. What's your first move?
title: The Stoic at the Gate

steps.scenario: The board flips to CANCELLED. A crowd forms at the desk. You…

options.text: Join the queue and tell everyone how unacceptable this is.
options.feedback: Totally human. But the anger costs you energy and changes nothing about the plane.

options.text: Open the airline app and rebook while you stand in line.
options.feedback: You spotted what's yours: your next choice. Whether a seat appears isn't; the queue stays a backup.

options.text: Sit down and wait for someone to announce a plan.
options.feedback: Calm is good. Pair it with one small action and you'll often get a better seat sooner.

steps.scenario: The agent says the next flight is tomorrow. You feel heat in your chest. You…

options.text: Breathe, then ask: 'What are my options for tonight?'
options.feedback: Same disappointment, better question. Calm, specific asks usually get more help than blame.

options.text: Tell the agent this is their fault.
options.feedback: Understandable, but they didn't cancel the plane. Blame aimed at the wrong target rarely pays.

options.text: Say nothing and walk off fuming.
options.feedback: Better than blaming the agent, but you left without the one thing you could still get: your options for tonight. Ask first, fume later.

insight: You didn't stop caring about getting home. Even the rebooking might fail; what stays yours is how you judge it and what you choose next. That's Epictetus's dichotomy of control.
model: When things go wrong, separate what's yours (judgment, choice, next action) from what isn't (the outcome).
try_today: Next time something annoys you, say out loud "What's mine here?" and do that one thing first.
try_team: When a plan falls through (match rained off, trip delayed, deadline moved), go round: each person names one 'what's ours here?' move before anyone vents.

from_source.quote: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things.

hook: Do you spend your week on what you can change, or what you can't?
title: Your Circle of Influence

questions.q: When the news is bad (prices, jobs, the world), I mostly…

options.label: Keep reading about it and feel worse
Read a bit, then try to step away
Ask what, if anything, changes for me this month

questions.q: When someone in my group project, team or family keeps letting things slide, I…

options.label: Vent about it to someone else
Wait and hope it improves
Ask them what's getting in the way

questions.q: My most common sentence starts with…

options.label: "If only they would…"
"I'll see what happens…"
"I can…" or "I'll try…"

questions.q: When I'm stuck, I first look for…

options.label: Who or what is to blame
Whatever I did wrong
The person who knows most about it
The smallest thing I could change

zones.label: Concern-heavy today
zones.text: Today a lot of energy went to things you can't move. That's tiring, and common when you're stressed, not a flaw. Pick one worry and find the smallest piece of it that's yours.

zones.label: Split today
zones.text: Today's answers switch between worrying and acting. Notice which topics pull you outward and give those one small action.

zones.label: Influence-focused today
zones.text: Today's answers aim at what you can move. Covey's claim is that this circle grows as you use it: trust and skill pile up.

insight: Covey drew two circles: what you care about, and the smaller part you can affect. Acting inside the small one builds skill and trust, so it tends to grow. A lens, not a lab finding.
model: Work inside what you can influence, and that circle slowly gets bigger.
try_today: Swap one "If only they…" sentence today for "I can…" and finish it with a real action.

source.work: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989); Epictetus, Discourses I.1 (c. 108 CE)

try_team: Draw two circles on a board. List the group's frustrations, place each one, then pick one item inside 'influence' to act on this week.

from_source.quote: What then? We must make the best use that we can of the things which are in our power, and use the rest according to their nature.
from_source.cite: Epictetus, Discourses, Book I, ch. 1 (trans. George Long, 1890)
from_source.next_read: Discourses, Book I, ch. 1 'Of the things which are in our power'

hook: Everyone's angry about it. Hardly anyone knows who decides.
title: Find the Door You Can Push

steps.scenario: Your town plans to close the library (or youth club, or park café) you love. Your group chat is furious. You…

options.text: Post an angry rant and share every petition you see.
options.feedback: Caring is good, and petitions can help. But anger online rarely reaches the people who actually decide.

options.text: Find out who decides, and when, then go or write to them.
options.feedback: You found the edge of your circle: the meeting, the inbox, the vote. That's where concern turns into influence.

options.text: Shrug: 'Nothing I can do about the council.'
options.feedback: Understandable, and sometimes true. But you measured your circle before testing it. It's often bigger than it looks.

steps.scenario: You spoke up. They close it anyway. You still care. You…

options.text: Decide speaking up was pointless and stop bothering.
options.feedback: It stings. But you met people and learned how decisions get made. That influence stays with you.

options.text: Keep arguing in the chat about whose fault it is.
options.feedback: Very human. Blame keeps you in the concern circle, though, where nothing moves.

options.text: Start something in reach: a book swap, a reading group at a café.
options.feedback: This is Covey's point. One door closed, so you pushed one you could open. Accepting a loss and acting can go together.

insight: Covey's circles are a lens, not a study. Research on 'locus of control' links believing your actions matter with better coping, though it's mostly correlational.
model: Before you give up or blow up, find who decides, and which part of it is yours.
try_today: Pick one thing that frustrates you. Spend 5 minutes finding out who actually decides it and how to reach them.
try_team: Pick a shared gripe (a rule, a schedule, a chore). Find out who decides it, then draft one short, specific request together.

source.work: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989); Rotter, Psychological Monographs (1966)

hook: Too timid or too reckless? Five calls will place your courage.
title: The Golden Mean

questions.q: Someone in your group (class, family, team) says something you think is wrong. You…

options.label: Wait, then ask a calm question in private
Stay quiet, it's not worth it
Say calmly, in front of everyone, that you see it differently
Call it out bluntly on the spot

questions.q: A friend invites you on a hard hike, longer than any you've done. You…

options.label: Say yes, then check the route and weather
Decline; you've never done one that long
Say yes and pick the harder route to push yourself

questions.q: Someone in your class or team is cheating (a test, a report) in a way that hurts others. You…

options.label: Drop a vague hint that people might notice
Confront them in front of everyone
Ignore it, it's not your business
Tell the teacher or manager privately

questions.q: You want to start something of your own (a channel, a club, a small business). You…

options.label: Put your savings and every free hour in from day one
Keep it in a notebook for 'someday'
Try a small version on weekends

questions.q: Someone is being mocked in a group chat. You…

options.label: Message them privately only
Say "not cool, stop" in the chat right away, then message them privately
Say nothing
Screenshot it and post it publicly to call the mocker out

zones.label: Leaning cautious today
zones.text: Today's answers lean cautious. Caution protects you, and sometimes it costs you. Try one small, safe step past your comfort line this week.

zones.label: Near the mean today
zones.text: Today's answers sit near the mean in these cases. Notice the mean was sometimes the bolder answer: Aristotle's mean is what the situation asks for, not the halfway point.

zones.label: Leaning bold today
zones.text: Today's answers lean bold. That energy is useful; adding one check before you leap turns boldness into courage.

insight: Aristotle put courage between cowardice and rashness. The mean is 'relative to us', not the midpoint: sometimes it's bold, sometimes a quiet no. Practical wisdom (phronesis) finds it.
model: Virtue is calibration: the right action, in the right amount, at the right time.
try_today: Pick one choice today and ask: what would 'too little' and 'too much' look like here? Then do the in-between.
try_team: Take a real decision your group faces. Write what 'too little' and 'too much' would look like, then agree on the right amount for this case.

from_source.quote: to feel them at the right times, with reference to the right objects, towards the right people... is what is both intermediate and best
from_source.cite: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, ch. 6 (trans. W. D. Ross, 1925)
from_source.next_read: Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, ch. 6-9; Book III, ch. 6-9 (on courage)

hook: Are you a better driver than most? Nearly everyone thinks so.
title: Knowing You Don't Know

game.question: In a classic study, what % of US university students who drive rated themselves more skilful than the typical driver in their group?
game.explain: Svenson (1981) found about 93% of a small sample of about 80 US university students rated themselves more skilful than the median driver in their group. At most 50% can be. Similar above-average ratings appear for many traits people value, though the size varies by trait and culture, and people often rate themselves below average on hard skills like juggling.

insight: Most of us rate ourselves above average, which can't all be true. Socrates thought himself wiser only in not claiming knowledge he lacked (Apology 21d). Rating yourself low is a guess too.
model: Treat your self-ratings, high or low, as guesses. 'I might be wrong' opens the door to learning.
try_today: Pick one opinion you hold strongly. Write the best reason someone could disagree with it, in their words, not yours.

source.work: Plato, Apology (c. 399 BCE); Svenson, Acta Psychologica (1981)

try_team: Each person writes one thing the group is sure of. Swap papers and write the best reason it might be wrong. Discuss the strongest one.

from_source.quote: he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know.

hook: You use it every day. Bet you can't explain it in 3 steps.
title: The Zip Test

game.prompt: Rate yourself 1-10: how well do you get how a zip works? Now explain it, out loud, in 3 steps. Go. Done? Did your rating just drop?
game.reveal: Engineers drop too: explaining is the test, not the job title. In Rozenblit & Keil (2002), most people's ratings dropped after they tried to explain. Feeling familiar isn't understanding.

insight: Familiar things feel understood until you try to explain them. Socrates found the same in Athens: people skilled at one craft assumed they knew far more. Explaining is the honesty test.
model: If you can't explain it step by step, you know less than it feels. Say it out loud to find out.
try_today: Explain something you rely on (a system at work, an app, a school topic) in 5 steps. Note where you said 'and then it just…'.
try_team: In a group (friends, family, a study group or team), each person explains one thing they 'know' in 2 minutes. Others may ask 'how exactly?' once.

source.work: Plato, Apology (c. 399 BCE); Rozenblit & Keil, Cognitive Science (2002)

from_source.quote: because they were good workmen they thought that they also knew all sorts of high matters
from_source.next_read: Plato, Apology 21b-23b (Socrates questions politicians, poets and craftsmen)

hook: A setback you got through: would you delete it from your story?
title: Amor Fati: Love Your Fate

game.prompt: Pick a real setback from your past: a rejection, a failure, a loss you've recovered from. If a button could erase it, and everything it led to, would you press it?
game.reveal: There's no wrong answer, and some pain is never 'worth it'. But many people find a setback also taught them a skill, a friend, or a direction. Nietzsche called embracing your whole story, hard parts included, amor fati. If you chose erase, that is honest too: some losses teach nothing worth their price.

insight: Amor fati isn't pretending bad things were good. In Ecce Homo Nietzsche wanted nothing different; you can start smaller: ask what a hard chapter gave you, or simply that you survived it.
model: You can't change what happened. You can choose what it becomes part of.
try_today: Write one setback and finish this line: "Because of it, I can now…". Keep it to one sentence.

source.work: The Gay Science (1882); Ecce Homo (1888), "Why I Am So Clever" §10; Meditations (c. 170 CE)

try_team: Each person shares one past setback and one thing it led to, in a sentence each. Listeners only say thanks: no advice, no fixing.

from_source.quote: Amor fati: let that henceforth be my love!
from_source.cite: Nietzsche, The Gay Science, §276 (trans. Thomas Common, 1910)
from_source.next_read: The Gay Science §276; Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book 4.1 (the fire image)

hook: What were you worried about on this date three years ago?
title: This Too Shall Pass

game.prompt: Try it now: what was keeping you up at night roughly three years ago? Can you name it clearly?
game.reveal: Whatever you answered, notice how today's weight compares. Wilson and Gilbert found we often predict bad events will hurt longer than they do, though the gap is smaller than first thought. Feelings are weather: real, sometimes heavy, but they move. If a heavy mood isn't lifting for weeks, talk to someone you trust.

insight: We often overestimate how long bad events will hurt (Wilson & Gilbert). Heraclitus saw a world in flux; the Buddha taught that clinging to what changes brings suffering.
model: Feelings and fortunes are weather, not climate. Ask how much this will matter in a year.
try_today: When something stings today, write it down with the date. Set a reminder to reread it in 3 months.

source.work: Wilson & Gilbert, 'Affective Forecasting' (2005); Levine et al., 'Accuracy in affective forecasting' (2012)

try_team: Each person recalls a worry from a year ago and rates, 0-10, how much it matters now. Compare the numbers out loud.

from_source.quote: You cannot step twice into the same rivers; for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you.
from_source.cite: Heraclitus, fragment 41, in John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1920)
from_source.next_read: Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy, ch. III (Heraclitus), fragments 41-50

hook: What do you want your mates to say on your 18th? Does this week match?
title: Begin With the End in Mind

questions.q: This week I gave real, undistracted time to people I love.
The people closest to me would say I show up for them.
This week I moved, slept and ate like someone I'd want to be in a few years.
I spent time on schoolwork, a sport or a hobby I'm actually proud of.
Someone has asked me for help with something I'm good at.
I did something this week that helped someone beyond my circle.
This month I helped someone without being asked.
I learned or practised something that's stretching me.
I did something this week I was not good at yet.

advice.0: Want a small next step for Relationships? Book 20 phone-free minutes with one person this week.
advice.1: Want a small next step for Health? Pick one: a 15-minute walk, or lights out 30 minutes earlier tonight.
advice.2: Want a small next step for Craft? Block one focused hour on the thing you'd want to be known for.
advice.3: Want a small next step for Contribution? Do one small useful thing for someone who can't repay you.
advice.4: Want a small next step for Growth? Choose one skill and practise it for 10 minutes today.

game.advice_even: Even shape. No single gap stands out. Ask which of the five you'd most regret neglecting by your 18th, and give it one 20-minute block this week.

insight: Covey pictured the speeches at your funeral; here it's a big birthday. Your shape shows one week, not your life: where to put attention next, not what you've failed at.
model: Decide what you want said about you at the end, then plan this week backwards from it.
try_today: Write three words you'd want your mates to use about you at your 18th. Plan one action for each this week.

source.work: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989); On the Shortness of Life (c. 49 CE)

try_team: Each person writes three words they'd want said about the group (class, team or club) in a year. Pick the most neglected one and plan one step.

hook: A long life, counted in weeks. More or fewer than you'd guess?
title: Your Life in Weeks

game.question: How many weeks are there in an 80-year life?
game.explain: 80 years × about 52.18 weeks ≈ 4,174. Seneca: a life is measured by how it is used, not how many weeks it holds. Burkeman's point isn't to rush or count losses, but to choose a few things that matter. For most adults many of these are work weeks, so one well-guarded week counts. Whatever your age, don't count backwards; pick one good week.

insight: About 4,000 weeks feels short, and if that feels heavy, that's normal. The point isn't to scare you but to sharpen you. Seneca said life is long enough if used well.
model: Time is finite and countable. Spend weeks the way you'd spend something precious.
try_today: Open your calendar or plans for next week. Block 2 hours for the one thing you'd be proud of, before other stuff fills it.

source.work: Four Thousand Weeks (2021); On the Shortness of Life (c. 49 CE)

try_team: Each person names the one thing this week they'd regret skipping. Share them, then help each other protect the time for it.

from_source.quote: life, if you know how to use it, is long.
from_source.cite: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life, 2.1 (trans. John W. Basore, 1932)
from_source.next_read: On the Shortness of Life, chapters 1-3

hook: That petty argument: would it survive one honest question?
title: The Grudge-Shrinking Question

steps.scenario: A teammate took a problem with your work straight to the boss without talking to you first. They're away from tomorrow for two weeks. You…

options.text: Ignore their messages until they apologise.
options.feedback: Fair to be hurt, but two weeks of silence usually makes the hurt grow, not shrink.

options.text: Message: 'Still a bit annoyed about that, but have a good break. Can we talk when you're back?'
options.feedback: You stayed honest and kept the door open. If this were your last message to them, you'd be glad it was this one.

options.text: Complain about them in the team group chat.
options.feedback: It feels good for a minute, then becomes one more thing to repair.

steps.scenario: In a meeting, a teammate presents part of your idea as their own. You'll work together all next month. You…

options.text: Say nothing, and quietly hold it against them for months.
options.feedback: Swallowed grudges leak out later and cost you months of easy teamwork.

options.text: Call it out in front of everyone at the next meeting.
options.feedback: You're right to want credit, but public blame tends to start a feud.

options.text: Tell them privately, calmly, and agree how you'll credit each other's work.
options.feedback: Memento mori doesn't mean swallowing it. It means fixing it without letting it eat your month.

steps.scenario: Your sister rings on your birthday. You haven't really spoken since a falling-out over a family holiday last year. You…

options.text: Thank her warmly and suggest lunch soon.
options.feedback: She reached out; you met her. The old topic can wait for a calmer day, face to face.

options.text: Keep it short and cool. She knows what she did.
options.feedback: Understandable, but a cool reply can turn one more year into five.

options.text: Raise the old disagreement right away to clear the air.
options.feedback: Clearing the air matters, but a birthday call is rarely the moment.

insight: Memento mori means 'remember you will die'. The Stoics used it not to frighten but to shrink the petty: which grudges matter at the end? It made the honest, kind step clearer.
model: Before you hold a grudge, ask: if this were our last talk, how would I want it to end?
try_today: Pick one small, stale grudge and send one warm, low-pressure message. You don't have to settle everything.
try_team: Before a tense meeting or family talk, each person writes: 'In a year, what will I wish I'd said here?' Share one line each, then begin.

from_source.quote: Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. ... While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.
from_source.cite: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book IV.17 (trans. George Long, 1862)
from_source.next_read: Meditations, Book II.11 and Book IV.17-19

hook: Moving next month. Guess who most people pick for one last half hour.
title: Short Time, Clear Choices

game.prompt: In a classic study, younger adults imagined moving far away in a few weeks, with one free half hour. Who did most of them pick to spend it with?
choices: A close friend or family member
Someone new they'd really clicked with
The author of a book they loved
game.reveal: The familiar face. Older adults in Fredrickson & Carstensen (1990) mostly chose a close partner; younger adults spread their picks until they imagined a move. There's no wrong personal choice here; this is about what most people did.

insight: When time feels short, through age, a move, or illness, people turn toward who matters most (Carstensen's research). It tracks felt time, not age. Memento mori borrows that clarity early.
model: A sense of limited time points you toward what matters. You can borrow it without waiting for an ending.
try_today: Name one person you'd make time for if you moved next month, or someone you'd like to know better. Send a short hello today.

source.work: Fredrickson & Carstensen, 'Choosing Social Partners', Psychology and Aging (1990)

try_team: Ask: 'If this were our last month together as a class, team or family, what would we stop, and what would we make time for?' Pick one of each.

from_source.quote: Every day, therefore, should be regulated as if it closed the series, as if it rounded out and completed our existence.
from_source.cite: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 12 'On Old Age' (trans. R. M. Gummere, 1917)
from_source.next_read: Moral Letters, Letter 12 'On Old Age' and Letter 101 'On the Futility of Planning Ahead'

hook: Nodding along keeps the peace. Does it keep the friendship?
title: Honest and Kind at Once

steps.scenario: Your friend sends you a song they wrote and asks, 'Be honest, should I post it?' The verses are great. The chorus drags. You…

options.text: 'It's amazing, post it now!'
options.feedback: Kind in the moment, but they asked for honesty and won't get the chance to make it better.

options.text: 'The verses are great. The chorus could be tighter. Want ideas?'
options.feedback: True and warm. They hear what works, what to fix, and that you're on their side.

options.text: 'Honestly? The chorus is boring.'
options.feedback: It's true, but with nothing kind next to it, it's hard to hear and easy to resent.

steps.scenario: Your family is planning the same holiday as every year. You'd love to try something different, but nobody's asked you. You…

options.text: Go along, then quietly sulk the whole week.
options.feedback: Staying quiet feels safe, but the feeling leaks out anyway and nobody knows why.

options.text: Say, 'Can I suggest something different this year? Here's why it matters to me.'
options.feedback: You said what you want without attacking the old plan. Now there's something real to talk about.

options.text: Announce you're not coming this year.
options.feedback: It's honest, but it skips the conversation that might get you what you want.

steps.scenario: In a group project or team meeting, everyone loves a plan. You can see a real flaw, but speaking up feels awkward. You…

options.text: Stay quiet and hope it works out.
options.feedback: If the flaw is real, it shows up later, when it's harder and costlier to fix.

options.text: 'I like this. One worry: here's the gap. Can we test it first?'
options.feedback: You named the problem, credited the idea and offered a next step. That's easy to say yes to.

options.text: Message someone afterwards that it's going to fail.
options.feedback: The worry is fair, but said behind the group it can't help the plan and costs trust.

insight: Each best move said the true thing and kept the relationship. Silence and bluntness feel easier but cost more later. Proverbs and Plutarch said it long before Brené Brown's 'clear is kind'.
model: Clear is kind: say the true thing, with care, to the person who needs to hear it.
try_today: Pick one thing you've only been hinting at. Say it plainly and kindly in one sentence, starting with what you value.

source.work: Dare to Lead (2018); The Gifts of Imperfection (2010)

try_team: Before deciding on a plan, everyone writes one honest worry on a card. Read them out without names, then pick one to test together.

from_source.quote: Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
from_source.next_read: Plutarch, How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend (Moralia)

hook: Big client pitch tomorrow. Is 'win it' the goal making you worse?
title: Aim at What's Yours

game.prompt: Two managers pitch the same client tomorrow. Ana's goal: 'Win the contract.' Ben's: 'Open with their problem, ask three sharp questions, make our case clearly.' Who's likelier to walk in steadier?
choices: Ana: a big goal fires you up
Ben: his goal is fully in his hands
game.reveal: Ben, most likely. In a golf study, players trained on process goals ('smooth tempo') kept nerves and focus steadier than those chasing a score (Kingston & Hardy, 1997). Ana still wants a fair thing; she's just aiming at something the client controls. Evidence is from small sport studies, not boardrooms: a strong hint, not a law.

insight: Wanting the win is fine. Aiming only at it is the trap: the client decides that, not you. Aim at moves you control and let the outcome be a hope.
model: Keep the outcome as a hope; make the goal something you fully control.
try_today: Rewrite tomorrow's scariest goal as actions: not 'get the yes' but 'open with their problem, ask three questions'.
try_team: Stand-up, 5 min: each person splits their top goal into 'what we'll do' and 'what we hope happens'. Tomorrow, report only on the first.

source.work: Cicero, De Finibus III (45 BCE), the archer image; Kingston & Hardy, 'Effects of different types of goals', The Sport Psychologist (1997)

hook: A bad quarter makes every job ad look like an escape hatch.
title: The New-Job Glow Fades

steps.scenario: Rough quarter: a project slipped and your boss is tense. A recruiter offers a similar role for a bit more pay. Your gut says 'anywhere but here'. You…

options.text: Say yes this week, before the feeling fades.
options.feedback: The urge is real, and sometimes it's right. But a call made at the bottom of a bad quarter judges the climate by one storm.

options.text: Make two lists: what's been bad for 6+ months, and what's only this quarter.
options.feedback: Weather vs climate. Long-running problems are good reasons to move; this quarter's storm may pass by itself.

options.text: Turn it down without looking: leaving feels disloyal.
options.feedback: Loyalty is a fair value. Still, ruling it out unseen lets today's mood decide for you, just in the other direction.

steps.scenario: Months later you hire someone great. Week 3, they beam: 'Best job I've ever had.' When do you book a proper 'how's it really going?' 1:1?

options.text: At their annual review.
options.feedback: A common default. By then the glow has often faded and quiet doubts have had months to grow unasked.

options.text: Around months 6 to 12, when the new-job glow tends to dip.
options.feedback: Right. Managers who switched jobs reported a satisfaction spike that slid back within about a year (Boswell et al., 2005).

options.text: No need: they're clearly happy.
options.feedback: Their joy is real; enjoy it. It's also a honeymoon, so plan the check-in before the dip, not after.

insight: New jobs bring a 'honeymoon' high, then a 'hangover' within about a year (Boswell et al., 2005). Good and bad patches at work pass. Judge the pattern, not the patch.
model: Before a big work decision, ask: is this weather (a patch) or climate (a pattern)?
try_today: List what's frustrating you at work and tag each item 'weeks' or 'months'. Tackle one from the months list first.
try_team: Retro, 5 min: everyone puts this sprint's pain points on stickies. Sort into 'one-off storm' and 'keeps coming back'. Fix one that keeps coming back.

source.work: Boswell, Boudreau & Tichy, 'The relationship between employee job change and job satisfaction: the honeymoon-hangover effect', Journal of Applied Psychology (2005)

hook: Your mates feel permanent. Want the actual number?
title: The School-Days Countdown

game.question: You're 16 and you all leave school at 18. Roughly how many school days do you have left with your mates?
game.explain: About 380. Not a countdown to panic over, a reason to say yes to Friday's plan. A school year is roughly 190 days (UK; about 180 in the US), so two years is about 380. Moving to college at 16 instead? Then it's this year that counts.

insight: Final-year students nudged to see graduation as close got happier and did more of what they'd miss (Kurtz, 2008; one small study). 'Last' can sharpen joy, not just dread.
model: Count what's left, not to panic but to notice: ordinary days become worth showing up for.
try_today: Text one mate a plan for this week: chips after school, a kickabout, revision at yours. Name the day now.
try_team: Class or family, 5 min: each person names one thing they'd regret not doing together before this year ends. Pick one and put it in the diary.

source.work: Kurtz, 'Looking to the future to appreciate the present', Psychological Science (2008); Seneca, On the Shortness of Life (c. 49 CE)
